subject: Banking
title: The Bank of Banks
description: One-minute skill: The Bank of Banks.

hook.text: Central banks don't serve ordinary people. They serve banks. The Federal Reserve is JPMorgan's bank.

buildup.text: Commercial banks hold reserve accounts at the central bank, just like you hold an account at a commercial bank.

discovery.text: Central banks clear interbank payments, set reserve requirements, and provide emergency loans.

twist.text: Before central banks, banking panics happened regularly.

climax.text: Central banks exist because banking systems need a backstop. Someone has to be the bank that never runs out of money.

punchline.text: The bank's bank. Central banks backstop the entire financial system.

quiz.question: Who are central banks' primary customers?

details.summary: Central banks serve as the bank for commercial banks, holding their reserves, processing interbank payments, and providing emergency lending when no private institution will. This role is the backbone of the entire financial system.
details.whyItMatters: Without a bank of banks, there is no trusted institution to settle transactions between banks or provide emergency liquidity during panics. This unique role makes central banks indispensable to financial stability.
takeaways: Commercial banks hold reserve accounts at the central bank
Interbank payments settle through the central bank's system
Emergency lending prevents bank failures from cascading

faq.question: Why do banks need a bank of their own?
faq.answer: When Bank A's customer sends money to Bank B, the banks need a trusted intermediary to move the funds between them. The central bank provides this settlement service through its reserve system, ensuring every transaction is final.

faq.question: What happens during a bank panic without a central bank?
faq.answer: Before central banks, panics caused cascading failures as banks called in loans from each other. The Panic of 1907 paralyzed the US financial system until J.P. Morgan personally organized a private rescue, motivating the creation of the Fed.
